items.followUp: Write any two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: One correct physical property of non-metals is worth one mark.
rubric.description: States one physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award for any one valid property, such as dull appearance, brittleness, or poor conductivity of heat or electricity.

rubric.why: The question requires two properties.
rubric.description: States a second, distinct physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award if a second valid property is given; do not award twice for the same property.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are generally dull (non-lustrous).
Solid non-metals are generally brittle and break easily.

items.followUp: Name any four elements belonging to the halogen family.

rubric.why: A halogen name earns credit toward the required list.
rubric.description: Names two halogens.
rubric.how: Award one mark for any two correct halogen names.

rubric.why: The answer should identify the halogens, not merely one or two examples.
rubric.description: Names at least four halogens.
rubric.how: Award the second mark for four correct names from fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine.

modelAnswer: The halogens are fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine.

items.followUp: Give two examples of highly reactive metals.

rubric.why: One suitable example earns one mark.
rubric.description: Gives one example of a least reactive metal.
rubric.how: Accept a valid example such as gold, silver, platinum or copper.

rubric.why: Two examples are required.
rubric.description: Gives a second, distinct example of a least reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award if two different valid examples are named.

modelAnswer: Gold and silver are examples of least reactive metals.

items.followUp: Write balanced equations for the reactions of hydrogen with oxygen and nitrogen.

rubric.why: The chlorine reaction must show the correct products and balanced equation.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced reaction of hydrogen with chlorine.
rubric.how: Award for H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl.

rubric.why: The iodine reaction must show the correct products and balanced equation.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced reaction of hydrogen with iodine.
rubric.how: Award for H2 + I2 → 2HI.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen reacts with chlorine: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl.
Hydrogen reacts with iodine: H2 + I2 → 2HI.

items.followUp: Name four isotopes and state one application of each.

rubric.why: Radioisotopes have important medical applications.
rubric.description: Gives a valid medical application of an isotope.
rubric.how: Award for a correct isotope-use pair, such as cobalt-60 for cancer treatment or iodine-131 for thyroid treatment.

rubric.why: Carbon-14 is used to estimate the age of old materials.
rubric.description: Gives the isotope application in dating.
rubric.how: Award for carbon-14 used to determine the age of fossils or archaeological remains.

rubric.why: Some isotopes are used as fuels in nuclear reactors.
rubric.description: Gives a valid nuclear-energy application.
rubric.how: Award for uranium-235 used as nuclear fuel or in nuclear fission.

rubric.why: A further distinct application is needed to cover the requested examples.
rubric.description: Gives another valid application of an isotope.
rubric.how: Accept, for example, phosphorus-32 in plant research or sodium-24 for tracing blood circulation; the overall answer should contain at least five applications.

modelAnswer: Cobalt-60 is used in the treatment of cancer.
Iodine-131 is used to diagnose or treat thyroid disorders.
Carbon-14 is used to determine the age of fossils and archaeological remains.
Uranium-235 is used as fuel in nuclear reactors.
Phosphorus-32 is used in research on the uptake of fertilizers by plants.

items.followUp: Classify molecules as monoatomic, diatomic, triatomic and polyatomic, giving an example of each.

rubric.why: A monoatomic molecule contains one atom.
rubric.description: Explains monoatomic molecules and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award for identifying one atom per molecule and a valid example such as He.

rubric.why: A diatomic molecule contains two atoms.
rubric.description: Explains diatomic molecules and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award for identifying two atoms per molecule and an example such as H2 or O2.

rubric.why: A triatomic molecule contains three atoms.
rubric.description: Explains triatomic molecules and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award for identifying three atoms per molecule and an example such as H2O or CO2.

rubric.why: A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms.
rubric.description: Explains polyatomic molecules and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award for identifying more than three atoms per molecule and a valid example such as NH3 or CH4.

rubric.why: Examples should correctly illustrate the different molecule types.
rubric.description: Correctly matches examples to molecule types.
rubric.how: Award for a set of valid examples representing the four types; accept other scientifically correct examples.

modelAnswer: Molecules are classified according to the number of atoms they contain.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; for example, He.
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; for example, H2.
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; for example, H2O.
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; for example, NH3.

items.followUp: Write four properties of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally have relatively weak forces between their molecules.
rubric.description: States their generally low melting or boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for stating that covalent compounds generally have low melting and/or boiling points.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally lack mobile charged particles.
rubric.description: States that they are poor conductors of electricity.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they generally do not conduct electricity.

rubric.why: Most covalent compounds do not dissolve readily in water.
rubric.description: States their general insolubility in water.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they are generally insoluble or slightly soluble in water.

rubric.why: Covalent substances commonly dissolve in organic solvents and often occur as gases, liquids or soft solids.
rubric.description: Gives another valid property of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Accept solubility in organic solvents or their usual physical states as gases, liquids or soft solids.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.
They are usually insoluble in water.
They are often soluble in organic solvents and may exist as gases, liquids or soft solids.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature, concentration and particle size affect diffusion in liquids.

rubric.why: Diffusion occurs down a concentration gradient.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of concentration difference.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a greater concentration difference increases the rate of diffusion.

rubric.why: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of temperature.
rubric.how: Award for stating that increasing temperature makes diffusion faster.

rubric.why: Smaller particles generally move and diffuse more readily than larger ones.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of particle or molecule size.
rubric.how: Award for stating that smaller particles diffuse faster than larger particles.

rubric.why: The nature of the liquid affects how easily particles move through it.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of the liquid medium.
rubric.how: Award for stating that lower viscosity or a less dense medium generally allows faster diffusion.

rubric.why: The answer should explain the factors rather than merely list them.
rubric.description: Clearly links the factors to the rate or direction of diffusion.
rubric.how: Award for correctly explaining that diffusion proceeds from higher to lower concentration and that the listed conditions alter its rate.

modelAnswer: Diffusion in liquids depends on the concentration difference: a larger concentration gradient gives faster diffusion.
Increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of particles and makes diffusion faster.
Smaller particles generally diffuse faster than larger particles.
The nature of the liquid also matters; diffusion is generally faster in a less viscous liquid.
